programs.intro:
If your loved one is 21+ and enrolled in both Medicare and Medicaid, or qualifies for Medicaid long-term care due to needing daily help with bathing, dressing, or medication management, Community HealthChoices (CHC) provides comprehensive home and community-based services. Because CHC is a managed care program, your loved one gets coordinated services through one organization instead of juggling multiple providers.

CHC covers a wide range of services—including personal care, home health, attendant care, adult day services, pest eradication, educational support, and nursing facility care if needed. Services are individualized based on your loved one's needs assessment, ensuring the care plan fits their specific situation. As of 2026, the monthly income limit is $2,982 per person, and home equity up to $752,000 is exempt if your loved one lives there or intends to return.

steps.title: Initial Assessment

steps.title: Enrollment
steps.description: Once both clinical and financial eligibility are confirmed, the CAO will notify you, the PA IEB, and the Managed Care Organization (MCO) you have selected. You will then finalize your enrollment and work with your MCO to select a service coordinator and develop a care plan.

faqs.question: Can my loved one keep their house if it's worth more than the asset limits?
faqs.answer: Yes, your loved one can keep their primary home as long as the equity is under $752,000 in 2026, they live there, intend to return, or a non-applicant spouse or dependent lives there. Home equity above this limit may affect eligibility.

faqs.question: What if my loved one has intellectual or developmental disabilities?
faqs.answer: CHC does not cover intellectual or developmental disability services beyond supports coordination. These are handled through the DHS Office of Developmental Programs, which has separate waiver programs.

faqs.question: Can my loved one stay in their current nursing home if they're already there?
faqs.answer: If your loved one is in a nursing home paid for by Medicaid, they will be enrolled in Community HealthChoices (CHC). They can generally remain in their current nursing home, provided the facility is in their chosen Managed Care Organization's (MCO) network. CHC does not cover residents in state-operated facilities, such as state veterans' homes, which remain outside the CHC program.

faqs.question: How do we choose between different managed care organizations?
faqs.answer: After CHC approval, you'll select an MCO that will coordinate all services. Ask about provider networks, wait times, and specific services your loved one needs. Different MCOs serve different regions and may have varying availability.

faqs.question: What happens to my loved one's Medicare benefits under CHC?
faqs.answer: Medicare benefits remain completely separate from CHC. Your loved one keeps their Medicare coverage and providers. CHC only coordinates the Medicaid long-term services and supports.

faqs.question: Can I apply for CHC while my loved one is still in the hospital?
faqs.answer: Yes, hospital discharge planners often help initiate the CHC application process. This can help ensure services are in place before your loved one returns home or moves to a care facility.

faqs.question: What if my loved one's income is slightly over the $2,982 monthly limit?
faqs.answer: Your loved one may still qualify even if their income exceeds the limit. Pennsylvania offers pathways such as 'spend-down' or specific Medicaid planning strategies (like Qualified Income Trusts) to help applicants who are over the income threshold. The County Assistance Office will determine if their medical expenses can be used to meet eligibility requirements.

faqs.question: How often are services reassessed once my loved one is enrolled?
faqs.answer: CHC conducts periodic reassessments based on your loved one's changing needs. You can also request a reassessment if your loved one's condition changes or they need additional services.

programs.name: LIFE (Living Independence for the Elderly)
programs.tagline: Pennsylvania's all-inclusive care program (the state's PACE): full medical and long-term care so frail seniors 55+ can keep living at home instead of in a nursing facility.
programs.intro:
If your loved one is 55 or older, needs nursing-home level of care, but wants to keep living at home, Pennsylvania's LIFE program may cover everything — medical care, prescriptions, in-home help, and more — at little or no cost. LIFE is Pennsylvania's version of the national PACE model (Program of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly). One provider organization coordinates and pays for all of your loved one's care, so you are not juggling separate doctors, pharmacies, home aides, and insurers.

Everything is built around a local LIFE center your loved one attends as often as their care plan calls for. The team there — doctors, nurses, therapists, social workers, and aides — manages primary and specialty care, prescriptions, physical and occupational therapy, adult day services, personal and home care, meals, dental, vision, hearing, and transportation to the center and to medical appointments. If your loved one ever needs a hospital stay or nursing-facility care, LIFE covers that too.

To qualify, your loved one must be 55 or older, be certified by the state as needing a nursing-facility level of care, live in the service area of a LIFE provider, and be able to live safely in the community with LIFE's help when they enroll. Most participants qualify through Medicaid and pay nothing; people who are not eligible for Medicaid can still enroll and pay privately.

faqs.question: Is LIFE the same as the PACE prescription program?
faqs.answer: No. Pennsylvania uses two confusingly similar names. LIFE (Living Independence for the Elderly) is the all-inclusive medical and long-term care program described here — Pennsylvania's version of the national PACE model. The other 'PACE' (Pharmaceutical Assistance Contract for the Elderly) only helps pay for prescription drugs. Your loved one can look into both.

faqs.question: Does my loved one have to move into a nursing home to qualify?
faqs.answer: No — it's the opposite. To enroll, your loved one must be certified as needing a nursing-facility level of care but still be able to live safely at home with LIFE's support. The point of LIFE is to provide that level of care at home and at a local LIFE center so they can avoid moving into a facility.

faqs.question: How much does LIFE cost?
faqs.answer: Most participants are eligible for both Medicare and Medicaid and pay nothing — no premium, deductible, or copay for covered services. If your loved one has Medicare but not Medicaid, they can still enroll by paying the Medicaid portion privately, and people with neither can pay the full cost out of pocket.

faqs.question: Can my loved one keep their own doctor?
faqs.answer: Generally no. Because a single LIFE organization coordinates and pays for all care, your loved one uses that provider's team and network. If keeping a specific doctor matters, ask the LIFE provider whether that doctor is in their network before enrolling.

programs.name: PACE (Pharmaceutical Assistance Contract for the Elderly) in Pennsylvania
programs.tagline: Low-cost prescriptions for Pennsylvania seniors 65+ with limited income

localEntities.name: Statewide via Department of Aging; local PA MEDI sites

programs.intro:
If your loved one is 65+ and living on a fixed income in Pennsylvania, PACE can dramatically reduce their prescription costs. The program covers both generic and brand-name medications with co-pays of just $6 for generics and $9 for brand names, no monthly premium required.

To qualify, your loved one's previous year income must be $14,500 or less for a single person, or $17,700 for a married couple. The program has no asset limits, so your loved one's savings, home value, or investments won't disqualify them. However, they cannot be enrolled in Medicaid prescription benefits.

Important: This is Pennsylvania's prescription assistance program, not the national PACE long-term care program. If your loved one needs comprehensive medical and long-term care services (such as in-home care, therapies, and coordinated medical care), that is Pennsylvania's LIFE program, which is a separate benefit.

applicationNotes: If your loved one sold their home, all capital gains must be declared as income within two years of the sale date. If your loved one is already enrolled in the full Medicaid prescription benefit, they are not eligible for PACE/PACENET.

While income limits do not automatically adjust for inflation, the Pennsylvania General Assembly periodically passes legislation to update eligibility thresholds and implement moratoriums to protect seniors from losing eligibility solely due to Social Security cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs).

Eligibility is based on the previous calendar year's gross income. If your loved one's income varies, they will indeed be re-evaluated annually based on that previous year's earnings. Because income is based on the prior year, a recent drop in income will not result in immediate eligibility; they will need to wait until the next annual evaluation cycle to report their lower income.

faqs.question: Can my loved one apply if they own their home outright?
faqs.answer: Yes. PACE has no asset limits, so home ownership, savings accounts, or investments won't disqualify your loved one. Only income from the previous calendar year matters for eligibility.

faqs.question: What if my loved one is on Medicare Part D, can they still get PACE?
faqs.answer: Yes, your loved one can have Medicare Part D and PACE at the same time. However, they cannot be enrolled in Medicaid prescription benefits (Medical Assistance pharmaceutical benefits).

faqs.question: My loved one's income was higher last year but dropped this year, when can they apply?
faqs.answer: PACE eligibility is primarily based on the previous calendar year's gross income. However, if your loved one has experienced a significant, permanent change in income, the PACE program may offer a 'financial change of status' review. Instead of waiting until the next calendar year, call the PACE hotline at 1-800-225-7223 to explain the situation; they can determine if your loved one qualifies for a re-evaluation based on their current circumstances.

faqs.question: Does Social Security count toward the income limit?
faqs.answer: Yes, gross Social Security income counts, but Medicare premiums deducted from Social Security are excluded. The program looks at Social Security before Medicare Part B premiums are taken out.

faqs.question: Can I apply for my loved one if they can't manage the application themselves?
faqs.answer: The application process allows for assistance, but you'll need to call the PACE hotline at 1-800-225-7223 to discuss representing your loved one and what documentation may be required.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one needs a prescription that's not covered?
faqs.answer: PACE covers a wide range of medications through its comprehensive formulary. If your loved one takes a specific drug, you can check the online formulary on the PACE website to see if it is covered before applying. If a medication is not on the list, there is a formal exception process that your loved one's doctor can initiate on their behalf.

faqs.question: If my loved one moves to another state, can they keep PACE benefits?
faqs.answer: No. PACE requires Pennsylvania residency for at least 90 consecutive days before application and continued residency to maintain benefits. Moving out of state ends eligibility.

faqs.question: How long do PACE benefits last once approved?
faqs.answer: The program materials don't specify renewal requirements or benefit duration. Call 1-800-225-7223 to ask about renewal processes and how long benefits continue.

programs.name: Healthy Horizons (QMB, SLMB, QI)
programs.tagline: Save on Medicare costs: See if your loved one qualifies for Pennsylvania’s Healthy Horizons.

localEntities.name: Local CAO in each PA county

programs.intro:
If your loved one is 65+ with Medicare and struggling with out-of-pocket medical costs, Pennsylvania's Healthy Horizons program can help. This program offers different levels of assistance depending on income: the QMB tier can cover Medicare Part A and B premiums, deductibles, and coinsurance, while SLMB and QI tiers provide assistance with the Medicare Part B premium.

To qualify, your loved one must be entitled to Medicare Part A and meet income and resource limits. Because these calculations can include spousal income and assets, the financial picture may be complex, but the potential savings are significant for those who qualify.

contentSections.title: Program Tiers and Benefits
contentSections.content:
**QMB Categorically Needy:** Full Medicaid plus all Medicare Part A/B premiums, deductibles, and copayments covered. Income limit: $1,350/month individual, $1,824 couple. Assets: $2,000 individual, $3,000 couple.

**QMB Cost-Sharing Only:** Medicare Part A/B premiums, deductibles, and copayments covered (no other Medicaid benefits). Higher asset limits: $9,950 individual, $14,910 couple.

**SLMB:** Medicare Part B premium only ($185/month in 2026). Income up to 120% FPL. Assets: $9,950 individual, $14,910 couple.

**QI-1 and QI-2:** Medicare Part B premium only. QI-1 up to 135% FPL, QI-2 up to 175% FPL. Same asset limits as SLMB. Cannot have full Medicaid.

faqs.question: Can my loved one keep their house if it's worth more than the asset limit?
faqs.answer: Yes, the primary home is exempt from asset limits regardless of value, provided the applicant lives there. Only countable assets like bank accounts, stocks, and secondary vehicles count toward the current 2026 resource limits of $9,950 for an individual or $14,910 for a married couple.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one's income is too high for QMB but might qualify for SLMB?
faqs.answer: The County Assistance Office automatically screens for all tiers. If your loved one doesn't qualify for QMB (full benefits), they'll check SLMB and QI eligibility without you needing to file a separate application.

faqs.question: Does my loved one's spouse's income count even if the spouse isn't applying?
faqs.answer: Yes, spouse income and resources are always counted in the eligibility calculation. This is a common source of confusion and application denials. You must provide documentation for both spouses' finances.

faqs.question: Can my loved one get retroactive coverage for medical bills they already paid?
faqs.answer: SLMB and QI can be retroactive up to 3 months, but QMB cost-sharing benefits (premiums and deductibles) cannot be applied retroactively. Bring unpaid medical bills to your CAO when applying.

faqs.question: How much will this actually save on Medicare costs?
faqs.answer: At a minimum, Medicare Part B premium coverage saves $202.90 per month ($2,434.80 per year in 2026). Full QMB coverage adds significant protection by covering the Medicare Part A inpatient hospital deductible ($1,736 per benefit period), the annual Part B deductible ($283), and 20% coinsurance for doctor visits and outpatient services. For someone with regular medical needs, this can mean thousands of dollars in annual savings.

faqs.question: Can I apply for my loved one if they have dementia or can't handle paperwork?
faqs.answer: Yes, family members can apply on behalf of elderly loved ones. You'll need to provide legal documentation if you're the appointed representative, or the CAO can help determine what authorization is needed.

faqs.question: What if my loved one already has Medicare Supplement insurance?
faqs.answer: Healthy Horizons can work alongside Medicare Supplement plans, but the benefits may overlap. Your loved one might be able to drop expensive supplement coverage and save money while getting similar or better coverage through the state program.

faqs.question: How long does coverage last once approved?
faqs.answer: Coverage continues as long as your loved one meets eligibility requirements. The state will review eligibility periodically (usually annually), and you'll need to report changes in income or resources that might affect benefits.

programs.name: SNAP (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program)
programs.tagline: Monthly food support to help seniors stay healthy and independent at home.
programs.intro:
If your loved one is 60 or older and struggling to afford groceries, SNAP can help. Benefits are loaded onto an EBT card each month, which works like a debit card at most grocery stores, farmers' markets, and authorized online retailers like Amazon and Walmart.
The amount your loved one receives is based on their unique financial situation—including their household size, income, and allowable expenses like housing and out-of-pocket medical costs. While the maximum benefit for a single person in the 48 contiguous states is **$298 per month** (and **$546** for a two-person household), many households receive an amount tailored to their specific needs.
Pennsylvania makes it easier for seniors to qualify than younger adults. Even if your loved one's gross income is slightly above the standard limit, they may still qualify by using special 'net income' rules that account for high medical and housing expenses. Furthermore, Pennsylvania does not have an asset test for most SNAP applicants, meaning your loved one can typically maintain eligibility while owning their home, a car, and modest savings.

programs.savingsSource: USDA FY2026 maximum allotment for a one-person household in the 48 contiguous states and DC: $298/month, effective October 1, 2025 through September 30, 2026. The minimum for a one- or two-person household is $24/month. Actual amounts depend on household size, net income, and deductions; age affects deductions, not the maximum.

If your household is facing immediate food insecurity and meets specific low-income criteria, you may qualify for 'expedited processing,' which requires the state to provide benefits within 5 calendar days. Be sure to mention your emergency situation immediately when you apply.

faqs.question: Can my loved one keep their house and still get SNAP benefits?
faqs.answer: Yes. Your loved one's primary home doesn't count toward asset limits, regardless of value. They can also keep one vehicle and reasonable personal belongings without affecting SNAP eligibility.

faqs.question: What if my loved one's income is slightly over the limit but they have high medical bills?
faqs.answer: Even if your loved one's gross income is above the standard limit, they may still qualify. Seniors (60+) can deduct verified out-of-pocket medical expenses that exceed $35/month from their income. These deductions lower their countable income, often bringing them under the limit to qualify for benefits. Always apply; many seniors are surprised to find they are eligible after these deductions are applied.

faqs.question: Can I apply for SNAP on behalf of my elderly loved one?
faqs.answer: Yes, adult children can apply as authorized representatives if their loved one gives permission. You'll need to complete an authorized representative form and may need to attend the eligibility interview with or instead of your loved one.

faqs.question: How much will my loved one actually receive each month?
faqs.answer: It depends on net income after deductions. For example, a single senior with $1,500/month income and $200 in medical expenses might receive around $150/month. Use the COMPASS calculator for a personalized estimate before applying.

faqs.question: Can my loved one use SNAP benefits to buy groceries online?
faqs.answer: Yes. Pennsylvania SNAP recipients can use their EBT card for online grocery orders from Amazon, Walmart, and other approved retailers. Delivery fees aren't covered by SNAP, but the groceries are.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one lives with family but buys their own food?
faqs.answer: Only people who buy and prepare food together count as one SNAP household. If your loved one shops and cooks separately, they apply as a one-person household even if they live with relatives.

faqs.question: How often does my loved one need to renew SNAP benefits?
faqs.answer: Seniors often receive a longer certification period—typically 24 or 36 months—making it easier to maintain benefits without frequent paperwork. You will receive renewal notices in the mail with clear instructions on when to recertify. Keep an eye on your mail, as missing these notices can cause a gap in coverage.

faqs.question: Can my loved one get SNAP if they're already receiving Medicaid or Medicare?
faqs.answer: Yes. SNAP is a separate program from health insurance. Many seniors receive SNAP, Medicaid, Medicare, and other benefits simultaneously. Being on one program doesn't disqualify you from others.

faqs.question: How is SHIP different from insurance agents who say they help with Medicare?
faqs.answer: SHIP counselors are trained and certified but don't sell insurance, they provide unbiased guidance about all available options. When you apply, a care manager will conduct an assessment to confirm eligibility, which includes verifying that your loved one is homebound and lacks the support to prepare adequate meals.

Please keep in mind that these programs are not universally free or guaranteed to be delivered five days a week in every location. Delivery frequency and meal types vary significantly by county, and many programs are publicly funded and may request a voluntary donation. Due to high demand, some counties may also have waiting lists. Since Pennsylvania has 52 different Area Agencies on Aging, service availability depends on where your loved one lives. The best first step is to contact your local Area Agency on Aging to request an assessment and find out what is specifically available in your community.

faqs.question: Can my loved one get meals if they have family nearby who could help?
faqs.answer: Likely not. The program excludes people who have family or informal supports available for meals and shopping. The assessment will evaluate what help your loved one actually receives, not just what's theoretically available.

faqs.question: What if my loved one can still drive but just doesn't cook much anymore?
faqs.answer: They need to demonstrate they cannot prepare nutritious meals due to physical, mental, or emotional limitations, not just preference. The in-home assessment will evaluate their actual cooking ability and safety in the kitchen.

faqs.question: How much do the meals cost?
faqs.answer: Many counties provide meals at no cost, like York County. However, some counties may require payment based on financial need. Ask your local Area Agency on Aging about costs during the intake interview.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my loved one?

faqs.question: What if my loved one lives in assisted living or senior housing?
faqs.answer: They must live in a non-institutional home setting to qualify. Assisted living typically wouldn't qualify, but senior housing apartments might depending on the level of meal services already provided.

faqs.question: Is this the same as the Meals on Wheels I can donate to?
faqs.answer: It's the same type of service, but Pennsylvania's program is administered through 52 different Area Agencies on Aging with varying local providers. Some areas may contract with traditional Meals on Wheels organizations, others use different meal delivery companies.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one's condition changes after they start receiving meals?
faqs.answer: Contact your local Area Agency on Aging if your loved one's functional abilities improve significantly or if they no longer need the service. They'll reassess eligibility as needed.

faqs.question: Can my loved one choose what meals they receive?
faqs.answer: Menus are planned by dietitians and certified by the PA Department of Aging, but they do accommodate medical conditions like diabetes and heart disease. Discuss dietary restrictions during your intake interview.

programs.intro:
If you're caring for a loved one 60+ with functional deficits or Alzheimer's in Pennsylvania, this program reimburses you for respite care, supplies, and other caregiving expenses. The reimbursement percentage depends on your loved one's household income, up to 100% for lower incomes, scaled down to 0% above 380% of the Federal Poverty Level ($60,648 for a household of one in 2026).

You pay upfront for approved services and submit receipts for reimbursement. Beyond financial help, the program provides care management, caregiver education, and training at no cost regardless of income. An in-home assessment determines what services you're authorized to receive.

The program also covers caregivers 55+ raising grandchildren or caring for disabled adult children (18-59) with different co-residence requirements. Each of Pennsylvania's 52 counties administers the program through their Area Agency on Aging, so services and wait times may vary by location.

faqs.question: Can I get reimbursed if my loved one's income is too high?
faqs.answer: If your loved one's household income is above 380% of the Federal Poverty Level ($60,648 for a household of one in 2026), you won't get financial reimbursement. However, you can still access non-financial services like care management, caregiver education, and training at no cost.

faqs.question: What expenses can I actually get reimbursed for?
faqs.answer: The program reimburses for respite care, supplemental services, consumable supplies, and other care-related expenses approved by your care manager. The specific services must be authorized during your in-home assessment. You cannot be reimbursed for hiring family members to provide care.

faqs.question: How long does it take to get my money back after submitting receipts?
faqs.answer: Reimbursement timelines vary by county since each Area Agency on Aging processes payments differently. Ask your local AAA about their typical processing time when you apply.

faqs.question: Can I apply if I'm caring for my spouse who has Alzheimer's?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your spouse has Alzheimer's or a related disorder at any age, you qualify as long as you both live in Pennsylvania and you're the primary caregiver. There's no relation or co-residence requirement for Alzheimer's care.

faqs.question: What if my loved one lives in one Pennsylvania county but I live in another?
faqs.answer: Both you and your care receiver must live in Pennsylvania, but you don't need to live in the same county. Contact the Area Agency on Aging in your loved one's county of residence since that's where they'll receive services.

faqs.question: Can I use this program and Medicaid waiver services at the same time?
faqs.answer: Generally, individuals enrolled in Medicaid Long-Term Services and Supports (such as Community HealthChoices or the LIFE program) are not eligible for the Caregiver Support Program, as those programs already provide comprehensive caregiving support. If your loved one is considering enrolling in a Medicaid waiver, discuss how this may impact your eligibility for the Caregiver Support Program with your local Area Agency on Aging during your initial assessment.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one's income changes after I'm enrolled?
faqs.answer: Your reimbursement percentage is based on your loved one's current household income, so changes may affect your reimbursement rate. Report income changes to your care manager who will adjust your reimbursement percentage accordingly.

faqs.question: Do I need to live with my loved one to qualify for this program?
faqs.answer: For caring for someone 60+ with functional deficits or anyone with Alzheimer's, you don't need to live together or be related. Co-residence is only required for caregivers 55+ caring for grandchildren under 18 or disabled adults 18-59.

OPLAP provides attorneys who specialize in elder law issues, from fighting benefit denials to defending against guardianship proceedings.

Eligibility is generally based on 125% of the federal poverty level (about $1,900/month for a single person in 2026), with priority given to seniors with the greatest economic and social needs. The program covers legal matters related to abuse, age discrimination, healthcare, housing, long-term care, Medicaid, Medicare, nutrition, Social Security/SSI, and utilities. Your loved one pays only court filing fees, attorney services are free.

High demand means many qualified seniors can't be served immediately. At least 80% of legal needs among low-income older adults go unmet nationally due to limited resources.

faqs.question: What if the facility retaliates against my loved one after I file a complaint?

programs.name: Aged, Blind, and Disabled Medicaid
programs.tagline: If your parent is 65 or older and on a fixed income, Pennsylvania's ABD Medicaid can cover their doctor visits, home care, and potentially nursing home costs at little or no cost to them.

localEntities.name: Pennsylvania Department of Human Services Medical Assistance program

programs.intro:
Pennsylvania's Aged, Blind, and Disabled (ABD) Medicaid is the state's health coverage program for people 65 and older, or any age if they are blind or disabled. For qualifying families, it pays for doctor visits, hospital care, home health services, personal care assistance, and, for those who need it, nursing home care. This is not a small supplement: for families whose parent needs daily help or is heading toward a nursing facility, ABD Medicaid can cover tens of thousands of dollars in annual care costs.

The program runs on three separate eligibility tracks, and that is where most families get confused. The regular track covers basic medical care for lower-income individuals (income limit: $22,025 per year for a single person). The medically needy track helps people whose income is higher but whose medical bills reduce their usable income below $425 per month. The long-term care track applies when your parent needs a nursing home or home-and-community services, and it carries a higher income limit of $2,982 per month (2026). Each track has different income rules, resource rules, and covered services.

This is one of the most paperwork-intensive programs in Pennsylvania, and decisions made before you apply, particularly gifts or asset transfers in the past 60 months, can affect eligibility for the long-term care track. Apply as early as possible. Processing takes up to 30 days, sometimes 45. Your County Assistance Office (CAO) handles all applications and can tell you which track your parent qualifies for.

The medically needy track uses a spend-down calculation: your parent's income above $425 per month counts as a deductible that must be met with medical bills before coverage begins. This math is complex; ask the CAO to walk through it with you.

For the long-term care track, gifts or transfers of assets made within the past 60 months are reviewed. Even transfers that seemed routine, such as helping a grandchild with college or adding someone to a deed, can create a penalty period that delays Medicaid coverage. Get this information on the table before you apply.

contentSections.title: Three tracks, three sets of rules
contentSections.body:
ABD Medicaid in Pennsylvania is not one program with one income limit. It has three distinct tracks.

Regular ABD Medicaid covers basic health care. Income limit: $22,025 per year for one person ($1,835/month). Asset limit: $2,000 for one person.

Medically Needy covers people whose income is higher but who have large medical bills. Net income after bills must fall below $425 per month (or $2,550 over a 6-month period) for one person.

Long-Term Care track applies when your parent needs nursing home care or home-and-community services at a nursing facility level. Income limit: $2,982 per month for one person (2026). Asset limit: $2,000, plus a $6,000 resource disregard if income is at or below that limit. This track has the 60-month transfer lookback and stricter asset review rules.

contentSections.title: What Medicaid does and does not pay in a care facility
contentSections.body: For qualifying long-term care participants, ABD Medicaid can pay for nursing home care, home health services, personal assistance, and transportation. It can also cover some medical services delivered inside an assisted living residence. It does not pay for room and board in assisted living, even when the resident qualifies for Medicaid on other grounds. This distinction matters significantly when families are weighing care options.

faqs.question: My parent's income is $2,400 per month. Is that too high to qualify?
faqs.answer: It depends on which track applies. For regular ABD Medicaid, the income limit is $22,025 per year ($1,835/month) for one person, so $2,400 per month would exceed that limit. However, the long-term care track allows income up to $2,982 per month (2026 limit), so your parent may still qualify if they need nursing home care or home-and-community services at a nursing facility level. The medically needy track is a third option if their medical bills bring their usable income low enough. Ask your County Assistance Office which track fits your parent's situation.

faqs.question: Can my parent keep their house if they apply for the long-term care track?
faqs.answer: In many cases, yes. The primary home is generally exempt from the asset count if a spouse, a child under 21, or a blind or disabled child lives there. Even if your parent enters a nursing home, the home may still be protected in certain circumstances. However, Pennsylvania does review home equity for some long-term care rules, and the home may be subject to Medicaid estate recovery after your parent's death. These rules are complex and situation-specific; consult with an elder law attorney or ask your County Assistance Office for a full explanation before making any decisions about the property.

faqs.question: My parent gave money to family members two years ago. Does that disqualify them?
faqs.answer: Possibly, for the long-term care track. Pennsylvania reviews all asset transfers or gifts made within the past 60 months (five years) when someone applies for long-term care Medicaid. A transfer that was not for fair market value can create a penalty period, meaning Medicaid will not pay for care for a set number of months. The penalty does not apply to the regular ABD or medically needy tracks. Disclose all transfers to the County Assistance Office when you apply; not disclosing them can cause bigger problems later.

faqs.question: Can a family member apply on behalf of an aging parent?
faqs.answer: Yes. A family member who holds a valid power of attorney can apply on a parent's behalf. Bring the legal POA document when applying in person or uploading through COMPASS. If no legal document exists, the County Assistance Office can explain what options are available based on your parent's capacity and situation.

faqs.question: My parent is in assisted living. Will ABD Medicaid pay for their care there?
faqs.answer: Partly. Medicaid can cover some medical services provided to your parent inside an assisted living residence, but it does not pay for room and board in assisted living. This means the facility's monthly base cost stays out-of-pocket or must be covered through other means. If the cost of assisted living is becoming unmanageable, ask the County Assistance Office whether a nursing facility or a home-and-community waiver program might be a better fit financially.

faqs.question: Can my parent apply for ABD Medicaid and SNAP at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is worth doing both at once. Many people who qualify for ABD Medicaid also qualify for SNAP food benefits. Both programs are handled through Pennsylvania's County Assistance Offices, and you can apply for multiple benefits through the COMPASS portal at compass.dhs.pa.gov in a single session.

faqs.question: How long will the application actually take?
faqs.answer: Pennsylvania is required to decide within 30 calendar days of a completed application. If the agency cannot finish in 30 days, it must notify you in writing and may extend to 45 days. The most common reason applications drag past 30 days is missing documentation. Submit every requested document as quickly as possible and keep copies of everything you send. If you have not heard anything after 30 days, call (800) 692-7462 to ask for a status update.

faqs.question: What happens after my parent is enrolled and their health needs change?
faqs.answer: Enrollment is not permanent without review. Pennsylvania conducts periodic eligibility renewals, and your parent's coverage must be redetermined at regular intervals. If your parent's income, assets, or care needs change significantly, such as moving from home care to a nursing facility, notify the County Assistance Office promptly. Changes that affect the track your parent is enrolled in can change what is covered and what documents are needed.

programs.name: LIHEAP
programs.tagline: If your parent pays heating bills on a fixed income in Pennsylvania, they may qualify for a cash grant paid directly to their utility or fuel provider, plus emergency help if heat is ever at risk.
programs.intro:
LIHEAP (Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program) helps Pennsylvania households with low to moderate incomes pay their heating costs. If your parent qualifies, Pennsylvania pays a cash grant directly to their utility company or fuel provider, so the money never needs to pass through your parent's hands. The grant amount varies by household size, income, and the type of fuel they use; the state does not publish a single fixed amount for all households.

Your parent does not need an overdue bill or a shutoff notice to apply for the regular cash grant. They can own or rent their home. There is no age requirement. The income limit for a single-person household is $23,940 per year (150% of the Federal Poverty Guidelines for the current season). A one-time $100 supplemental payment was also announced for eligible households in 2026, paid automatically to the utility or fuel provider without a separate application.

Pennsylvania also has a separate crisis component for households facing a genuine heating emergency, such as a broken furnace or an imminent shutoff. Crisis assistance is handled through local County Assistance Offices and works differently from the regular grant. Both components are available only during the open LIHEAP season, so timing your application matters.

contentSections.title: Your parent does not need a crisis to qualify
contentSections.body: Many families only contact LIHEAP when a shutoff notice arrives. But the regular cash grant has no such requirement. Your parent can apply during the open season simply because their income qualifies, and Pennsylvania will pay their utility or fuel company directly. Waiting until there is an emergency limits your options.

contentSections.title: What the benefit actually looks like
contentSections.body: Pennsylvania does not publish a single fixed grant amount. The cash grant varies based on three factors: household size, gross annual income, and the type of fuel your parent uses to heat their home. The benefit is sent directly to the utility company or fuel vendor; your parent will see a credit on their account rather than receiving a check. The 2026 one-time $100 supplemental payment works the same way: it goes to the utility or fuel provider automatically, with no separate action needed from your parent.

faqs.question: My parent is a renter and heat is included in their rent. Can they still apply?
faqs.answer: Yes. Pennsylvania LIHEAP allows renters whose heat is included in their rent to apply. The household must be responsible for heating costs either directly (paying a utility or fuel bill) or indirectly (heat built into the rent). Your parent should apply and note on the application that heat is part of their lease.

faqs.question: My parent's furnace broke and they have no heat right now. Do they use the regular application?
faqs.answer: No. A heating emergency is handled through the crisis assistance component, which is separate from the regular cash grant. Call your parent's local County Assistance Office immediately; do not use the standard online or phone application for this situation. Find the local CAO at pa.gov/agencies/dhs.

faqs.question: Can I apply on my parent's behalf, or does my parent have to apply themselves?
faqs.answer: You can apply on your parent's behalf. When you apply through COMPASS or by phone, you can identify yourself as the person completing the application on behalf of the household. Have your parent's Social Security number, income documents, and heating bill ready. Call 1-866-857-7095 if you have questions about completing the application as a representative.

faqs.question: The LIHEAP season just opened. How quickly should we apply?
faqs.answer: Apply as early as possible. LIHEAP funding is limited. There is no statewide waitlist described in official materials, but early applications are assigned to caseworkers faster. Processing typically takes up to 30 days after a caseworker is assigned, so applying early in the season gives the most lead time before cold weather becomes urgent.

faqs.question: My parent already received a LIHEAP grant. Do they get the $100 supplemental payment automatically?
faqs.answer: According to Pennsylvania DHS, the 2026 one-time $100 supplemental payment is automatic for eligible households; no separate application is required. The payment goes directly to the utility or fuel provider. If you are unsure whether your parent qualifies or want to confirm the payment was made, call the LIHEAP Hotline at 1-866-857-7095.

faqs.question: My parent's income went up this year. Are the income limits the same as last year?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Pennsylvania's LIHEAP income limits update each program year to reflect the current Federal Poverty Guidelines. The limit for a single-person household in the current season is $23,940 per year (150% FPL). Always verify the current season's figures at pa.gov/agencies/dhs/resources/liheap before assuming your parent qualifies or does not qualify based on a prior year's limits.

programs.name: Property Tax/Rent Rebate Program
programs.tagline: Pennsylvania reimburses your parent up to $1,000 a year on property taxes or rent paid, if their income is under $48,110.

programs.intro:
If your parent is 65 or older, owns a home or rents in Pennsylvania, and has an annual income under $48,110, they may qualify to get money back on what they paid in property taxes or rent last year. The rebate is not a monthly check; it is a once-a-year payment from the Pennsylvania Department of Revenue. Depending on income, that payment can be as high as $1,000.

The amount depends on where your parent's income falls in a four-tier table. Someone earning $8,550 or less per year can get up to $1,000 back. Someone earning between $19,241 and $48,110 can get up to $380. Both homeowners and renters qualify, though renters need their landlord to sign a Rent Certificate form (PA-1000 RC) before they can apply.

One detail many families miss: this program looks at last year's income and last year's taxes or rent, not what your parent is paying today. And approval does not carry over; your parent must file a new claim every single year using form PA-1000.

faqs.question: My parent earns about $22,000 a year. How much will they actually get back?
faqs.answer: At $22,000, your parent falls in the $19,241 to $48,110 income tier, which has a standard maximum rebate of $380. That is the most they can receive at that income level under the standard formula. If they own a home and their property taxes exceed 15% of their total income, an enhanced calculation may apply automatically when they file, potentially increasing the rebate.

faqs.question: My parent rents. Can they still apply, or is this only for homeowners?
faqs.answer: Renters can apply and receive the same rebate amounts as homeowners. The requirement is that their landlord must sign the PA-1000 RC Rent Certificate, which documents the rent paid in the prior year. Ask the landlord to complete this form before you start the application; without it, the application will be incomplete.

faqs.question: My parent already qualified last year. Do they automatically get the rebate again this year?
faqs.answer: No. This program requires a new PA-1000 application every single year. Last year's approval does not carry over. If your parent misses a year, they lose that year's rebate entirely. Set a reminder to file each year.

faqs.question: My parent's income dropped a lot this year because of medical bills and reduced hours. Will the program use this year's lower income?
faqs.answer: No. The rebate is always calculated on prior-year income and prior-year property taxes or rent paid. If your parent's income dropped this year, that lower income will be used when you apply next year for the following rebate cycle. The current application reflects what happened last year.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my elderly parent if they cannot manage the paperwork themselves?
faqs.answer: Yes. A family member or authorized representative can help complete and submit the PA-1000 on the parent's behalf. If your parent has a power of attorney or legal guardian, that documentation may be requested. For questions about representative filing, call 1-888-222-9190.

faqs.question: Does owning a home with significant equity or savings in the bank disqualify my parent?
faqs.answer: No. This program has no asset limit. It is income-based only. Your parent's home value, savings, or investments do not affect eligibility or the rebate amount. Only their annual income and what they paid in property taxes or rent the prior year are considered.

faqs.question: My parent is 62 and widowed. Do they qualify?
faqs.answer: Not yet. Widows and widowers qualify at age 50 or older, so your parent does qualify as a surviving spouse. The age 65 requirement applies to the general population; the 50-plus threshold applies specifically to widows and widowers. They will need documentation such as a death certificate or marriage certificate to confirm their status.

faqs.question: Can my parent apply for this rebate and also apply for LIHEAP or SNAP at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes. The Property Tax/Rent Rebate Program is entirely separate from LIHEAP (utility bill help) and SNAP (food benefits). Receiving one does not affect eligibility for the others. Many Pennsylvania seniors with low incomes qualify for all three. Applying for them at the same time is common and encouraged.

programs.name: State SSI Supplement
programs.tagline: Pennsylvania adds a monthly cash payment on top of federal SSI, up to $394/month more for seniors in personal care homes.
programs.intro:
If your parent already receives SSI, or would qualify for SSI except that their income is slightly too high, Pennsylvania pays them an additional monthly cash supplement. The exact amount depends on where your parent lives: seniors living at home alone receive $27.40/month extra, while those in a personal care boarding home can receive up to $394.30/month on top of their federal SSI payment.

This supplement is not a separate application in most cases. SSA determines SSI eligibility first, and Pennsylvania's supplement follows automatically based on living arrangement. The one exception is for residents of domiciliary care homes and personal care boarding homes, where the local Area Agency on Aging handles part of the process using form PA-761.

Your parent cannot be in a public institution or a Medicaid-paid facility where Medicaid covers more than 50% of care costs. If they are living at home, in someone else's household, or in a licensed personal care home, they are likely in an eligible setting.

steps.title: Receive combined payment
steps.description: For most recipients, SSA issues one combined check that includes both the federal SSI amount and the Pennsylvania supplement. You will not receive two separate payments.

applicationGuide.processingTime: No single statewide standard. SSA processes the underlying SSI claim first; the supplement follows that determination. SSI processing can take several months, longer if a disability determination is required.
applicationGuide.tip: If your parent's income is slightly above the SSI limit, do not assume they are ineligible. Pennsylvania can pay a supplement even when federal SSI is denied due to excess income in some cases. Ask SSA directly.

applicationNotes: If your parent moves from living alone into a personal care boarding home, the supplement amount increases significantly but you must notify SSA and the Area Agency on Aging. The change is not automatic.

People who are denied SSI because their income is too high may still qualify for the state supplement in some cases. Do not stop the process after an SSI denial without asking SSA specifically about the Pennsylvania supplement.
The supplement is not counted as income for SSI eligibility purposes, so receiving it does not push your parent over any income threshold.

faqs.question: My parent's income is slightly too high for SSI. Can they still get the Pennsylvania supplement?
faqs.answer: Possibly yes. Pennsylvania can pay a state supplement to people who would be eligible for SSI except that their income is too high, depending on the specific rules for their living arrangement. Do not assume a prior SSI denial closes this door. Call SSA at 1-800-772-1213 and ask specifically whether your parent qualifies for the Pennsylvania supplement despite excess income.

faqs.question: If my parent moves from their own apartment into a personal care home, do we need to do anything?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it matters financially. Moving into a personal care boarding home changes the supplement from $27.40/month to $394.30/month for an individual. You must notify SSA of the change in living arrangement and contact the local Area Agency on Aging to complete form PA-761 for the facility-based supplement. The increase is not applied automatically.

faqs.question: Will my parent receive two separate checks, one from SSA and one from Pennsylvania?
faqs.answer: Usually no. For most recipients, SSA issues one combined payment that includes both the federal SSI amount and the Pennsylvania supplement. Residents of domiciliary care homes and personal care boarding homes typically receive this single combined payment as well.

faqs.question: Does receiving this supplement affect my parent's SSI payment or Medicaid eligibility?
faqs.answer: No. Pennsylvania's supplement is not counted as income for SSI eligibility purposes, so it does not reduce the federal SSI payment. Medicaid eligibility rules are separate; ask your local county assistance office if you have questions about Medicaid specifically.

faqs.question: Can I apply for this supplement on behalf of my parent?
faqs.answer: Yes. A family member can apply on behalf of a parent who is unable to apply independently. SSA allows a representative to complete the SSI application process. If your parent has already appointed you as a representative payee or has legal documentation such as power of attorney, bring that when you call or visit.

faqs.question: What happens if my parent's living situation changes after they are enrolled?
faqs.answer: The supplement amount changes any time the living arrangement changes. Moving from living alone to living in someone else's home, or from home to a personal care facility, will adjust the payment up or down. You are required to report the change to SSA. Failure to report can result in overpayments that SSA will reclaim.

stateOverview.intro: Pennsylvania offers 9 programs that can save your aging loved one hundreds of dollars monthly and connect you with free support services. Six are qualification-based benefits, like Community HealthChoices covering up to 32 home care services, PACE providing low-cost prescriptions, or SNAP adding up to $300/month for groceries. Three are free resources available to all Pennsylvania seniors, including SHIP counseling to navigate Medicare and legal assistance through OPLAP. Most income-based programs use similar thresholds, so if your loved one qualifies for one, they may qualify for several. Start by checking the programs below that address your most urgent need, financial help, daily care support, or free guidance.

startHere.name: Community HealthChoices (CHC)
startHere.why: Covers the most expensive need, daily personal care and health services at home, if your loved one is dual eligible or needs daily assistance.

startHere.name: SNAP (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program)
startHere.why: Quick financial relief with up to $300/month for groceries, and eligibility often indicates qualification for other programs.

startHere.name: SHIP (State Health Insurance Assistance Program)
startHere.why: Free for everyone and can immediately identify Medicare cost savings your loved one may be missing.

quickFacts: Pennsylvania's Community HealthChoices program serves as the main pathway for Medicaid long-term care services, covering up to 32 different home and community-based services.
PACE prescription program is specific to Pennsylvania seniors 65+ and provides significant drug cost reductions beyond standard Medicare coverage.
Three free resource programs (SHIP, OPLAP, Long-Term Care Ombudsman) have no income limits and are available to any Pennsylvania senior or their family.
stateOverview.resourcesVsBenefits: Six programs require qualification based on income, age, or care needs, these provide direct financial assistance like Community HealthChoices covering home care services or SNAP providing grocery money. Three programs are free resources available to any Pennsylvania senior regardless of income, SHIP for Medicare guidance, OPLAP for legal help, and the Ombudsman for nursing home advocacy. Even if your loved one's income is too high for financial benefits, these free resources can still save money through better Medicare choices and problem resolution.
